title: B2B vs B2C Product Metrics: Why the Same Benchmark Means Different Things
description: Churn under 2%, NRR above 110%, LTV:CAC of 3–7×—these are B2B numbers. Using them in B2C is how PMs mislead their boards. Here's the full breakdown.
body:
A PM moves from Duolingo to Salesforce. Their first week, they pull the same retention dashboard they ran at their last company and show 40% monthly active users returning. Their new skip-level looks worried. "That's... actually concerning for an enterprise product."

Same metric. Opposite interpretation. Welcome to the B2B vs B2C divide.

Product metrics are not universal. The frameworks you learned at a consumer company will actively mislead you at an enterprise company, and vice versa. This guide maps the differences precisely, so you can stop applying the wrong benchmarks to your product.

## Why the Same Metric Means Different Things

The root cause of confusion is structural: B2B and B2C products have fundamentally different relationships between the person paying, the person using, and the person making the buying decision.

In **B2C**, the user is the buyer. They pay with their credit card, they use the product daily, and if they stop finding it valuable, they cancel. Metrics reflect this: acquisition cost, activation rate, daily engagement, voluntary churn.

In **B2B**, the buyer (the economic decision-maker) is often not the user (the employee), who is often not the champion (the internal advocate who pushed for the tool). A company can pay for Salesforce for three years even if individual sales reps hate using it, because the CFO signed a multi-year contract and the admin team configured the integration. Metrics reflect this structural complexity: expansion revenue, net revenue retention, seat utilization, renewal rate.

The product team's job in each context is different. B2C PMs fight for the user's attention every session. B2B PMs fight for the buyer's renewal every quarter while ensuring users actually adopt the product so the renewal is defensible.

## Engagement Metrics: The Same Name, Completely Different Benchmarks

### Daily Active Users / Monthly Active Users (DAU/MAU)

**B2C interpretation:** DAU/MAU (the "stickiness ratio") should be as high as possible. A consumer app with 50% DAU/MAU (users return on half of all days) is performing well. Facebook's ratio has historically been above 65%. If your B2C app's ratio drops below 20%, you have a product problem.

**B2B interpretation:** Many enterprise tools are weekly or monthly workflows by design. An expense reporting tool used once a week is working correctly. A contract management platform used monthly is fine. Applying B2C stickiness benchmarks to B2B tools creates false alarms and misallocated product investment.

**The right B2B question:** Are users completing their core job within the tool? What's the time-to-task-completion for the primary workflow? Session frequency is less important than workflow completion rate.

### Retention Rate

**B2C benchmark:** A consumer SaaS product with 10–15% monthly churn is struggling. Good B2C retention is under 5% monthly churn for subscription products. For freemium with a large free user base, the numbers shift dramatically.

**B2B benchmark:** B2B SaaS companies target under 1–2% monthly customer churn (roughly 10–20% annual churn), with best-in-class products at under 5% annually. But the more important metric is **net revenue retention (NRR)** — which accounts for expansion revenue. An NRR above 110% means your existing customers are spending more than they were a year ago, even after accounting for churned accounts. The top quartile of B2B SaaS products has NRR above 120%.

**The practical trap:** A B2B PM who reports "we have 85% retention" is often masking the real story. 85% customer retention with 70% revenue retention (because churned customers were larger) is much worse than 80% customer retention with 115% revenue retention (because expanding customers were much larger). Always pair customer retention with revenue retention in B2B reporting.

## Acquisition Metrics: Quantity vs. Quality of the Buyer

**B2C:** CAC (customer acquisition cost) and LTV (lifetime value) with a target LTV:CAC ratio of roughly 3:1. High volume of low-contract-value customers means unit economics must be tight. Payback period targets are often under 12 months.

**B2B:** The LTV:CAC ratio expectation is similar (3–7× is the common benchmark), but the numbers underneath are completely different. A B2B deal might cost $20,000 to acquire (enterprise sales cycles, legal reviews, security audits) but carry $200,000 in annual recurring revenue. Payback periods of 18–24 months are common and acceptable in enterprise, where contracts are multi-year.

The PM implication: B2B PMs need to understand which customer segments produce the best LTV (not just the most revenue at signing) and influence product decisions accordingly. A large enterprise that churns in year two is worse economics than a mid-market company that expands 40% annually.

## Feature Adoption: Individual vs. Organizational

In B2C, feature adoption is measured against your entire user base. If 30% of users use a new feature, that's either a win (if the feature was designed for a segment) or a problem (if it was supposed to be core).

In B2B, feature adoption has an additional layer: **seat penetration**. A company might have 500 Salesforce seats but only 200 active users. The 300 inactive seats represent both a churn risk and an expansion opportunity. B2B PMs track:

- **Seat utilization:** (Active users / licensed seats) × 100. Below 60% is a warning sign. Above 80% often signals expansion potential.
- **Feature adoption by persona:** The field sales rep, the sales manager, and the RevOps admin all use Salesforce differently. Feature adoption rates need to be segmented by persona to be meaningful.
- **Time-to-activation:** How long does it take a new employee (not a new company) to complete their first core task? Long time-to-activation predicts both individual churn and organizational dissatisfaction.

## North Star Metrics: Different Outcomes, Different Stars

The North Star Metric framework (a single metric that represents user value and predicts long-term growth) works in both B2B and B2C, but the metric itself looks different.

| Company | North Star | Why |
|---------|-----------|-----|
| Airbnb (B2C) | Nights booked | Captures value for both guests and hosts |
| Slack (B2B) | Messages sent per org per day | Predicts team stickiness and renewal |
| Duolingo (B2C) | Daily active learners | Engagement and habit formation |
| HubSpot (B2B) | Number of contacts managed | Value realization proxy, predicts expansion |
| Spotify (B2C) | Time listened | Core consumption metric |
| Salesforce (B2B) | CRM records updated weekly | User adoption at org level |

Notice that B2C North Stars tend to be individual engagement metrics (sessions, time, purchases). B2B North Stars tend to be organizational value metrics (records managed, workflows completed, seats active).

## The Metrics That Only Exist in B2B

Three metrics that have no meaningful B2C equivalent:

**Net Revenue Retention (NRR):** (Beginning ARR + expansion - contraction - churn) / Beginning ARR. This is the single best predictor of a B2B SaaS company's health. NRR above 100% means you grow even if you acquire zero new customers.

**Logo Churn vs. Revenue Churn:** You can lose many small customers (high logo churn) while retaining your largest accounts (low revenue churn). Or vice versa. Best practice is to track both separately and weight your concern by revenue impact.

**Time to Value (TTV):** How long from contract signing to the customer achieving their first measurable outcome? In enterprise B2B, long TTVs are the leading cause of churn — buyers get impatient, projects stall, and the incumbent wins the renewal by default. Shortening TTV is often more valuable than adding features.

## The Metrics That Only Exist in B2C

**K-Factor (viral coefficient):** The number of new users each existing user generates. For consumer products with viral loops (referrals, social sharing, network effects), a K-factor above 1.0 means the product grows without paid acquisition. Largely irrelevant in B2B, where buying cycles involve procurement and legal teams, not social sharing.

**Day-1/Day-7/Day-30 retention curves:** Consumer product teams obsess over cohort retention curves in the first 30 days because this is where most voluntary churn happens. The shape of the curve (gradual slope vs. sharp drop on day 3) tells you where the product loses people. B2B products have multi-week onboarding flows where a "day 7 user" may not have even completed setup yet.

**Viral loops and referral rates:** Consumer products live and die by organic growth. B2B products grow through sales motions, even in product-led growth (PLG) companies — the viral loop is PQLs (product-qualified leads) surfaced to a sales team, not direct peer-to-peer sharing.

## A Practical Checklist for PMs Switching Between B2B and B2C

If you're moving from a consumer role to enterprise (or vice versa), audit your mental model:

**B2C → B2B:**
- Replace DAU/MAU focus with seat utilization and workflow completion
- Add NRR and logo retention to your core dashboard
- Track expansion revenue separately from new ARR
- Learn to segment all metrics by customer tier (enterprise, mid-market, SMB)
- Build a stakeholder map for your top accounts — users, admins, economic buyers

**B2B → B2C:**
- Individual user retention replaces org-level metrics
- Acquisition funnels are higher volume, shorter cycles — think in days not quarters
- Every user is the economic buyer; there's no separate "champion" relationship
- Network effects and viral loops now matter to your growth model
- Price sensitivity and willingness to pay research is continuous, not annual
